articles.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
articles.description: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter.

articles.title: Anna Durbin speaks on a new understanding of infection models
articles.description: Most clinical trials ask how diseases can be fought. But what if the answer to this question relies on understanding how the disease begins and progresses? This is what Dr. Anna Durbin, Professor of International Health at the School of Public Health, spoke about in her talk "The Use of Controlled Human Infection Models to Evaluate Countermeasures for Dengue and Zika Virus" in the Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Department Seminar on Thursday, Oct. 29. Durbin opened her talk by defining what a controlled human infection model (CHIM) is. "We infect people with pathogens, and we follow the course of disease. And we do this for different reasons; we can do this to study… what the kinetics of an infection, for instance a viral infection, is, what the clinical manifestations are," she explained. "We typically use these in the evaluation of countermeasures such as vaccines and therapeutics." "We monitor these participants very closely. And I think the important part of a controlled human infection model is the word 'controlled,' because we control everything; we control the dose, we control the way that the pathogen is administered, we control how long it's been from, for instance, vaccination to challenge," she said. Durbin further categorized CHIMs into two different types: the disease model and the infection model. The disease model typically involves enteric pathogens - microbes that infect the gastrointestinal tract such as Salmonella or Shigella - and assesses the severity of disease in patients. This entails tracking symptoms and assigning disease scores. The infection model, on the other hand, is not focused on disease progression. Rather, it looks at the collection of the pathogen of interest at different times throughout an infection to understand when the microbe reaches certain concentrations within the host. She continued to explain that CHIMs are particularly useful to establish the efficacy of a therapeutic and a correlate of protection before bringing it to an expensive clinical trial stage. Historically, some vaccine candidates brought to the clinical trial stage have shown evidence of efficacy in mice or other animal models, but are ineffective when used in humans. A CHIM can ensure only therapies showing promising results are moved to the costly trial stage or can bypass trial stages altogether. She then transitioned into sharing some of the work done in her lab to develop a controlled human infection model for dengue, noting that the lack of adequate animal models for this infection make it a great candidate for work in humans. Durbin's group developed their CHIM using a virus strain that was originally developed for a live attenuated vaccine but was ultimately abandoned. They infected participants with 1000 infectious viral particles and collected blood samples for the detection of a virus at regular intervals for the following six months. They found that their infection model led to viremia - viruses in the blood - in all patients, as well as rash and reversible neutropenia in some, which is a decline in a kind of white blood cell. No severe disease was seen in any patients. With the model established, she then described how it has been used to evaluate the efficacy of a live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine developed by the NIH and determine which formulation should move forward to late-stage clinical trials. "Back in 2015, there was a live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine that was produced by Sanofi-Pasteur that induced what would be considered to be very good neutralizing antibody titers against all four viruses, but the vaccine failed to protect against dengue," she said. "That told us that neutralizing antibody is not necessarily predictive of protection, and that's again one of the reasons that we developed this challenge model." Using their model, Durbin's lab found that one of the vaccine formulations led to 100% protection against viremia and laid the groundwork for the recent licensing of a dengue vaccine in Brazil. This vaccine has now been approved for stage 3 clinical trials in multiple other countries, including the United States. She went on to share more projects done using the dengue CHIM. This included a clinical trial she claimed was her favorite from her work, which showed that a tetravalent vaccine which includes all four dengue subtypes - as opposed to a trivalent vaccine which only includes three subtypes - is necessary to protect people from dengue infection. She ended the talk with some of the work the lab has done setting up a CHIM for Zika virus since 2016. "We weren't sure that we would have enough [cases] really to understand the clinical manifestations of Zika as well as the kinetics of viral replication and shedding," she said. "We also thought it could be very useful for the evaluation of a Zika vaccine given that, again, the outbreak waned very quickly and now we continue to see small outbreaks of Zika, but it's unpredictable when and where they will occur." Durbin closed by acknowledging some of the future work she hopes to do using the Zika human challenge model, emphasizing the usefulness of CHIMs in getting therapeutics approved and understanding how viruses replicate within humans.

articles.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
articles.description: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
articles.description: Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday. The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities. articles.description: A new study published in Nature Materials reports that researchers have developed an aluminum gallium nitride device that combines light detection, memory and basic processing by controlling charge at polarization interfaces. The device can detect light at the nanowatt-per-square-centimeter level and operate stably at temperatures up to 300°C.

articles.title: A standard shortcut, used since the 1970s, hides a magneto-optic effect in ordinary glass fiber
articles.description: For more than 50 years, engineers have described light in optical fiber using a convenient shortcut, one that works so well it is rarely questioned. Engineers at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg, South Africa, have now shown that this shortcut hides a small but real effect. A magnet placed beside a multimode fiber, rather than along it, can change the light traveling inside.

articles.title: The psychology of saving electricity: How comparisons can curb consumption
articles.description: Simple psychological interventions are often enough to encourage people to change their behavior—and this is also true when it comes to saving electricity. A new study by Mannheim-based consumer psychologist Dr. Yavor Paunov and colleagues shows that comparing one's own electricity consumption with that of others as well as practical energy-saving tips can help reduce energy consumption.

articles.title: Microscopy upgrade sharpens images fivefold without sacrificing tissue imaging depth
articles.description: Researchers at Texas A&M University have cracked a problem that has limited biological imaging for years: seeing fine cellular detail while looking deep inside living tissue. The new microscopy technique resolves structures smaller than 100 nanometers, roughly a thousand times thinner than a human hair, without giving up the ability to image deep into intact samples.

articles.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
articles.description: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers.

articles.title: Prison data analysis finds choosing lowest reoffending risk scores preserves overall accuracy
articles.description: Whether an individual reoffends after their release from prison or is successfully rehabilitated depends on several factors. When assessing the risk of recidivism, all of these are taken into account—both by human experts and by machine learning models. If several equally reliable computational models produce different risk ratings, the lowest value should be used for the individual concerned, suggest Ashwin Singh (TU Wien) and Carlos Castillo (ICREA/Universitat Pompeu Fabra).

articles.title: How cells pull together: Theoretical study reveals a hidden source of attraction
articles.description: Imagine two people standing on a stretchy sheet. When one pulls, the other feels the fabric move and responds with a pull of their own. Each adjustment changes what the other feels. Something similar happens between living cells. They tug on the material around them, sense the stretching caused by their neighbors and adjust their own forces.

articles.title: Repeat thieves without kleptomania struggle to adapt to rewards in decision-making test
articles.description: Theft is almost universally considered an exploitative behavior. The conventional view underlying judicial systems is that the act of taking resources from others without offering compensation stems from moral and personal failings. As a result, these systems rely on the assumption that the threat or imposition of punishment will motivate criminal offenders to adjust their future behavior. Yet the outcome is not always success.

articles.title: Team designs molecules that efficiently generate orange-to-red light for OLED displays
articles.description: Most of us spend much of our day staring at organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs, which convert electricity into light to produce the colorful displays on smartphones, computer monitors and televisions. Although metal-free light-emitting materials that produce all colors are in demand, it has been difficult to make ones that efficiently emit orange-to-red light. Now, researchers led by the University of Osaka have shown that such materials do not need to be held in a rigid shape to work well: flexible molecules that can change shape can also emit orange-to-red light.
